target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would directly remove the work/school scheduling barrier to voting, especially for low-income workers
objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee private employers will close or provide paid time off, so retail and service workers may still have to work and may lose wages to vote. Because the people most likely to struggle are often in those jobs, the holiday would not consistently remove the scheduling barrier it is supposed to solve.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is unreliable because it does not force every private employer to provide paid leave
objection: The relevant effect is not universal paid leave, but the change in the default day itself. Making Election Day a national holiday shifts school and work routines, so many people can vote during holiday hours or with less need for extraordinary leave, which still meaningfully reduces the scheduling barrier.

target: AG1’s claim that changing the calendar date itself will reliably ease work/school conflicts
objection: The holiday does not necessarily change enough employer behavior to matter for low-income workers. Many retail and service employers can still schedule shifts on holidays, so workers may still face the same wage-vs.-voting tradeoff and the supposed calendar-level benefit may not hold uniformly.

target: AG2’s claim that private employers’ continued operation defeats the holiday proposal
objection: Even if some employers stay open, a holiday changes expectations across institutions, including holiday-aware staffing and scheduling norms. Voting becomes part of a known national holiday routine rather than a normal weekday interruption, which makes accommodations and time to vote more feasible.

target: AG2’s claim that OECD election timing cannot justify a U.S. holiday proposal
objection: The fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays shows that this kind of scheduling change is already used in practice. That comparative pattern undermines the claim that holiday timing cannot reliably reduce work/school barriers.

target: AG1’s inference that OECD holiday/weekend elections prove holiday timing itself causes better voting access
objection: OECD adoption does not show that holiday timing is the causal factor. Those countries may also have stronger labor protections, different work structures, or other voting reforms, so their experience does not prove that a U.S. federal holiday alone would reliably solve the access problem.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday fails because workers may still have to take a full unpaid day off
objection: Voting is time-bounded, not an all-day absence, and a holiday creates more usable voting windows before, after, or around shifts. So even if employers remain open, the holiday can still reduce the scheduling barrier by making part of the day available without wage loss.

target: AG1’s claim that workers will have usable voting windows once Election Day is a holiday
objection: A holiday does not guarantee that retail or service workers get a non-working interval overlapping polling hours, and polling hours do not automatically extend. If workers are still scheduled through the voting window, the holiday does not materially change the tradeoff.

target: AG2’s focus on employer leave rules as the main barrier
objection: The proposal also addresses school and caregiving logistics, not just paid leave. Closing schools and public services on Election Day reduces childcare and family-schedule conflicts that can otherwise force voters to lose wages or pay for last-minute care.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday still leaves the same last-minute wage tradeoffs
objection: A national holiday makes Election Day predictable and plan-able, which lets workers arrange coverage or shift swaps in advance rather than needing emergency unpaid leave. That predictability itself reduces the practical scheduling barrier.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday does not change the economic penalty of voting
objection: Holiday payroll and staffing practices often provide holiday pay, premiums, PTO use, or holiday coverage, so the cost of taking the small amount of time needed to vote is often less severe than on an ordinary weekday.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday pay and holiday scheduling make voting less wage-threatening
objection: Holiday pay usually compensates hours worked, not hours spent voting, and many low-income hourly workers have limited PTO and still face scheduled daytime shifts. So the economic tradeoff may remain largely unchanged even if the day is labeled a holiday.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is a weak and inequitable turnout reform
objection: A holiday would reduce the weekday scheduling barriers faced by low-income workers and parents because schools, public services, and workplaces would operate on holiday routines. That makes the reform a meaningful way to lower the work/school conflict that suppresses turnout.

target: AG1’s belief that schools/daycare and workplaces will reliably shift to holiday routines
objection: School and daycare arrangements will not reliably align with a federal holiday, and private employers are not required to stop scheduling retail or service workers. The holiday can therefore create new childcare costs or leave the wage-voting tradeoff essentially unchanged.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday will not reliably help low-income workers
objection: The policy directly targets the weekday work/school constraint by shifting school and caregiving routines and making work schedules holiday-aware. That lowers the need for last-minute childcare and coverage, which are major barriers for low-income voters.

target: AG1’s claim that school closures and holiday-aware scheduling reliably help low-income parents
objection: A federal holiday does not require employers to close or give paid time off, so many low-income parents would still work. If schools or daycare close while parents still have to work, the holiday can simply replace one conflict with another, such as childcare costs or the same wage loss.

target: AG2’s overall claim that the holiday cannot meaningfully reduce the scheduling barrier
objection: The important effect is that the holiday changes the default weekday calendar for schools and caregiving and makes voting time more predictable. That reduces the last-minute disruptions and wage penalties that most affect low-income workers with tight schedules.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday status will create real non-working periods and easier caregiving
objection: Many low-income workers in retail, restaurants, and other service jobs would still be scheduled during voting hours, and school closures can create backup-childcare needs that are costly or hard to fill. So the holiday does not reliably produce usable time or reduce caregiving burdens for the groups most constrained by hourly work.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers will still face the same tradeoff because employers may remain open
objection: The holiday changes more than employer closure rules: it shifts the timing of school and caregiving routines and makes the day predictable for shift planning. Because voting usually fits within an extended window rather than requiring a full day away from work, the holiday lowers the likelihood that people must sacrifice wages to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that school closures reduce caregiving disruption for low-income parents
objection: That assumes parents can absorb the remaining work and childcare constraints. If retail and service employers still run holiday shifts, school closures can force parents to find or pay for childcare on a day they still must work, so the holiday can turn the work/school conflict into a work/childcare-cost conflict instead.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday does not reliably reduce wage and childcare disruption costs
objection: The holiday changes the timing of both childcare demand and workplace routines, letting families line up voting with predictable holiday periods and reducing the need for emergency childcare or uncompensated time off. Even if some businesses stay open, holiday scheduling norms can lessen the work/childcare burden.

target: AG1’s claim that school closure plus holiday routines reduce childcare disruption enough to matter
objection: That assumes parents can stay home or find low-cost replacement care, but many low-income workers still must work when schools close and childcare may be unavailable or more expensive. So school closures alone do not reliably remove the economic penalty of voting or working on Election Day.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday fails to reduce wage/childcare costs in practice
objection: A national holiday shifts workplace routines and creates predictable holiday periods, so parents can often plan voting and childcare around those periods rather than scrambling for emergency coverage. That reduces the likelihood of wage-sacrificing or expensive replacement-care arrangements.
